00011| Welcome to the Next.js documentation!
00012| 
00013| ## What is Next.js?
00014| 
00015| Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.
00016| 
00017| It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.
00018| 
00019| Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.
00020| 
00021| ## How to use the docs
00022| 
00023| The docs are organized into 3 sections:
00024| 
00025| - [Getting Started](/docs/app/getting-started): Step-by-step tutorials to help you create a new application and learn the core Next.js features.
00026| - [Guides](/docs/app/guides): Tutorials on specific use cases, choose what's relevant to you.
00027| - [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference): Detailed technical reference for every feature.
00028| 
00029| Use the sidebar to navigate through the sections, or search (`Ctrl+K` or `Cmd+K`) to quickly find a page.
00030| 
00031| ## App Router and Pages Router
00032| 
00033| Next.js has two different routers:
00034| 
00035| - **App Router**: The newer router that supports new React features like Server Components.
00036| - **Pages Router**: The original router, still supported and being improved.
00037| 
00038| At the top of the sidebar, you'll notice a dropdown menu that allows you to switch between the [App Router](/docs/app) and the [Pages Router](/docs/pages) docs.
00039| 
00040| ### React version handling
00041| 
00042| The App Router and Pages Router handle React versions differently:
00043| 
00044| - **App Router**: Uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries) built-in, which include all the stable React 19 changes, as well as newer features being validated in frameworks, prior to a new React release.
00045| 
00046| - **Pages Router**: Uses the React version installed in your project's `package.json`.
00047| 
00048| This approach ensures new React features work reliably in the App Router while maintaining backwards compatibility for existing Pages Router applications.
00049| 
00050| ## Pre-requisite knowledge
00051| 
00052| Our documentation assumes some familiarity with web development. Before getting started, it'll help if you're comfortable with:
00053| 
00054| - HTML
00055| - CSS
00056| - JavaScript
00057| - React
00058| 
00059| If you're new to React or need a refresher, we recommend starting with our [React Foundations course](/learn/react-foundations), and the [Next.js Foundations course](/learn/dashboard-app) that has you building an application as you learn.
00060| 
00061| ## Accessibility
00062| 
00063| For the best experience when using a screen reader, we recommend using Firefox and NVDA, or Safari and VoiceOver.
00064| 
00065| ## Join our Community
00066| 
00067| If you have questions about anything related to Next.js, you're always welcome to ask our community on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/discussions), [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/bUG2bvbtHy), [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/nextjs), and [Reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/nextjs).

00017| It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.
00018| 
00019| Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.
00020| 
00021| ## How to use the docs
00022| 
00023| The docs are organized into 3 sections:
00024| 
00025| - [Getting Started](/docs/app/getting-started): Step-by-step tutorials to help you create a new application and learn the core Next.js features.
00026| - [Guides](/docs/app/guides): Tutorials on specific use cases, choose what's relevant to you.
00027| - [API Reference](/docs/app/api-reference): Detailed technical reference for every feature.
00028| 
00029| Use the sidebar to navigate through the sections, or search (`Ctrl+K` or `Cmd+K`) to quickly find a page.
00030| 
00031| ## App Router and Pages Router
00032| 
00033| Next.js has two different routers:
00034| 
00035| - **App Router**: The newer router that supports new React features like Server Components.
00036| - **Pages Router**: The original router, still supported and being improved.
00037| 
00038| At the top of the sidebar, you'll notice a dropdown menu that allows you to switch between the [App Router](/docs/app) and the [Pages Router](/docs/pages) docs.
00039| 
00040| ### React version handling
00041| 
00042| The App Router and Pages Router handle React versions differently:
00043| 
00044| - **App Router**: Uses [React canary releases](https://react.dev/blog/2023/05/03/react-canaries) built-in, which include all the stable React 19 changes, as well as newer features being validated in frameworks, prior to a new React release.
00045| 
00046| - **Pages Router**: Uses the React version installed in your project's `package.json`.
00047| 
00048| This approach ensures new React features work reliably in the App Router while maintaining backwards compatibility for existing Pages Router applications.
00049| 
00050| ## Pre-requisite knowledge
00051| 
00052| Our documentation assumes some familiarity with web development. Before getting started, it'll help if you're comfortable with:
00053| 
00054| - HTML
00055| - CSS
00056| - JavaScript
00057| - React
00058|

00060|

00062|

Welcome to the Next.js documentation!

## What is Next.js?

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. You use React Components to build user interfaces, and Next.js for additional features and optimizations.

It also automatically configures lower-level tools like bundlers and compilers. You can instead focus on building your product and shipping quickly.

Whether you're an individual developer or part of a larger team, Next.js can help you build interactive, dynamic, and fast React applications.

title: use cache
description: Learn how to use the "use cache" directive to cache data in your Next.js application.

The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async.

> **Good to know:**

The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async.

00002| title: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
00003| nav_title: PPR Platform Guide
00004| description: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
00005| related:

00007|   links:

00012| ---
00013| 
00014| Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a `postponedState` blob for each PPR-enabled route. At request time, the shell is served immediately and dynamic portions are rendered and streamed to the client.
00015| 
00016| This page explains how platforms can implement PPR support at different levels of sophistication.
00017| 
00018| ## How PPR Works
00019| 
00020| ### Build time
00021| 
00022| For each PPR route, Next.js produces:
00023| 
00024| - A **static HTML shell** containing all the content that can be prerendered, with [Suspense](/docs/app/guides/streaming#what-is-streaming) fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.
00025| - A **`postponedState`** value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering `postponedState` produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.
00026| - An **RSC payload** for the static portions of the page.
00027| 
00028| ### Request time
00029| 
00030| When a request arrives for a PPR route:
00031| 
00032| 1. The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.
00033| 2. The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.
00034| 3. Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.
00035| 
00036| The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.
00037| 
00038| ## Storing PPR Artifacts
00039| 
00040| Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:
00041| 
00042| 1. The static HTML shell.
00043| 2. The `postponedState` blob.
00044| 
00045| These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via [time-based](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) or [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.
00046| 
00047| Use [`requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2`](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter) in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.
00048| 
00049| ## Origin-Only Implementation
00050| 
00051| **This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.**
00052| 
00053| All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what `next start` does by default.
00054| 
00055| No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.
00056| 
00057| ## CDN Shell + Origin Compute
00058| 
00059| For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:
00060| 
00061| 1. The CDN serves the cached shell immediately (edge latency).
00062| 2. The CDN sends a resume request to the origin server (ideally in parallel with streaming the shell).
00063| 3. The origin server renders only the dynamic portions and streams them back.
00064| 4. The CDN concatenates the shell and dynamic content into a single streaming response to the client.
00065| 
00066| This requires the CDN to support a mechanism for combining cached and dynamic content in a single streaming response. The static shell TTFB drops to edge latency while dynamic content still streams from origin.
00067| 
00068| For the lowest possible latency, the shell can be served from edge storage (for example, a KV store populated during `onBuildComplete`) rather than from a CDN cache. This is a platform architecture decision and does not require any changes to the Next.js application.
00069| 
00070| ## The Resume Protocol
00071| 
00072| The **resume protocol** tells the Next.js handler to skip the shell and render only the dynamic portions. It is used by CDN-to-origin architectures and adapter-based deployments that serve the shell separately.
00073| 
00074| In standard `next start`, the server handles both the shell and dynamic render in a single pass automatically.
00075| 
00076| ### CDN-to-origin
00077| 
00078| When the CDN makes an HTTP request to a separate Next.js origin:
00079| 
00080| - Send a **POST** request to the route with the header `next-resume: 1`.
00081| - Include the `postponedState` blob as the **request body**.
00082| - The server will render only the deferred Suspense boundaries and stream the result.
00083| 
00084| > **Good to know:** When a POST request combines a Server Action with a PPR resume, the request body contains the postponed state followed by the action body. The `x-next-resume-state-length` header carries the byte length of the postponed state prefix so the handler can separate the two. For a pure PPR resume (the common case), the entire request body is the postponed state and this header is not needed.
00085| 
00086| ### Adapter-based
00087| 
00088| When the platform invokes the handler function directly:
00089| 
00090| - Call the entrypoint handler with `req.method` set to `'POST'`, the `next-resume: 1` header on the request, and the `postponedState` as the request body. (You can also pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` as the third argument to the handler invocation, which is equivalent but bypasses the HTTP layer entirely.)
00091| - The handler renders only the deferred Suspense boundaries and streams the result to `res`.
00092| - No HTTP round-trip is needed: the handler is invoked in-process.
00093| 
00094| ### Finding PPR routes in build output
00095| 
00096| In the [adapter output](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/output-types), PPR routes are identified by `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'` in the prerenders array. Iterate `outputs.prerenders` to find these entries and read `fallback.postponedState`.
00097| 
00098| `pprChain.headers` contains the headers needed for the resume protocol: `{ 'next-resume': '1' }`.
00099| 
00100| For detailed implementation with code examples, see [Implementing PPR in an Adapter](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter).
00101| 
00102| ## Implementation Checklist
00103| 
00104| 1. **Read PPR outputs at build time.** In your adapter's `onBuildComplete`, identify prerenders with `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'`. Store the shell HTML and `postponedState` in your cache.
00105| 
00106| 2. **Serve the shell at request time.** For incoming requests to PPR routes, serve the cached shell immediately and begin streaming.
00107| 
00108| 3. **Resume dynamic rendering.** For CDN-to-origin: send a POST request to the Next.js handler with the `next-resume: 1` header and the postponed state as the body. For adapter-based: call the handler directly with POST method and the postponed state in the request body (or pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` to the handler). Stream the response back to the client.
00109| 
00110| 4. **Handle cache updates.** Use `requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2` to capture new shell + postponed state pairs after revalidation, and update your cache atomically.
00111| 
00112| 5. **Support graceful degradation.** If the postponed state is unavailable or stale, fall back to a full server render. The user gets a complete page without the shell-first optimization.
00113| 
00114| For the complete adapter API reference and implementation examples, see the [Deployment Adapter API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath).
00115|

00014| Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a `postponedState` blob for each PPR-enabled route. At request time, the shell is served immediately and dynamic portions are rendered and streamed to the client.
00015| 
00016| This page explains how platforms can implement PPR support at different levels of sophistication.
00017| 
00018| ## How PPR Works
00019| 
00020| ### Build time
00021| 
00022| For each PPR route, Next.js produces:
00023| 
00024| - A **static HTML shell** containing all the content that can be prerendered, with [Suspense](/docs/app/guides/streaming#what-is-streaming) fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.
00025| - A **`postponedState`** value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering `postponedState` produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.
00026| - An **RSC payload** for the static portions of the page.
00027| 
00028| ### Request time
00029| 
00030| When a request arrives for a PPR route:
00031| 
00032| 1. The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.
00033| 2. The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.
00034| 3. Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.
00035| 
00036| The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.
00037| 
00038| ## Storing PPR Artifacts
00039| 
00040| Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:
00041| 
00042| 1. The static HTML shell.
00043| 2. The `postponedState` blob.
00044| 
00045| These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via [time-based](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) or [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.
00046| 
00047| Use [`requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2`](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter) in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.
00048| 
00049| ## Origin-Only Implementation
00050| 
00051| **This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.**
00052| 
00053| All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what `next start` does by default.
00054| 
00055| No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.
00056| 
00057| ## CDN Shell + Origin Compute
00058| 
00059| For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:
00060| 
00061| 1. The CDN serves the cached shell immediately (edge latency).
00062| 2. The CDN sends a resume request to the origin server (ideally in parallel with streaming the shell).
00063| 3. The origin server renders only the dynamic portions and streams them back.
00064| 4. The CDN concatenates the shell and dynamic content into a single streaming response to the client.
00065| 
00066| This requires the CDN to support a mechanism for combining cached and dynamic content in a single streaming response. The static shell TTFB drops to edge latency while dynamic content still streams from origin.
00067| 
00068| For the lowest possible latency, the shell can be served from edge storage (for example, a KV store populated during `onBuildComplete`) rather than from a CDN cache. This is a platform architecture decision and does not require any changes to the Next.js application.
00069| 
00070| ## The Resume Protocol
00071| 
00072| The **resume protocol** tells the Next.js handler to skip the shell and render only the dynamic portions. It is used by CDN-to-origin architectures and adapter-based deployments that serve the shell separately.
00073| 
00074| In standard `next start`, the server handles both the shell and dynamic render in a single pass automatically.
00075| 
00076| ### CDN-to-origin
00077| 
00078| When the CDN makes an HTTP request to a separate Next.js origin:
00079| 
00080| - Send a **POST** request to the route with the header `next-resume: 1`.
00081| - Include the `postponedState` blob as the **request body**.
00082| - The server will render only the deferred Suspense boundaries and stream the result.
00083| 
00084| > **Good to know:** When a POST request combines a Server Action with a PPR resume, the request body contains the postponed state followed by the action body. The `x-next-resume-state-length` header carries the byte length of the postponed state prefix so the handler can separate the two. For a pure PPR resume (the common case), the entire request body is the postponed state and this header is not needed.
00085| 
00086| ### Adapter-based
00087| 
00088| When the platform invokes the handler function directly:
00089| 
00090| - Call the entrypoint handler with `req.method` set to `'POST'`, the `next-resume: 1` header on the request, and the `postponedState` as the request body. (You can also pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` as the third argument to the handler invocation, which is equivalent but bypasses the HTTP layer entirely.)
00091| - The handler renders only the deferred Suspense boundaries and streams the result to `res`.
00092| - No HTTP round-trip is needed: the handler is invoked in-process.
00093| 
00094| ### Finding PPR routes in build output
00095| 
00096| In the [adapter output](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/output-types), PPR routes are identified by `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'` in the prerenders array. Iterate `outputs.prerenders` to find these entries and read `fallback.postponedState`.
00097| 
00098| `pprChain.headers` contains the headers needed for the resume protocol: `{ 'next-resume': '1' }`.
00099| 
00100| For detailed implementation with code examples, see [Implementing PPR in an Adapter](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter).
00101| 
00102| ## Implementation Checklist
00103| 
00104| 1. **Read PPR outputs at build time.** In your adapter's `onBuildComplete`, identify prerenders with `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'`. Store the shell HTML and `postponedState` in your cache.
00105| 
00106| 2. **Serve the shell at request time.** For incoming requests to PPR routes, serve the cached shell immediately and begin streaming.
00107| 
00108| 3. **Resume dynamic rendering.** For CDN-to-origin: send a POST request to the Next.js handler with the `next-resume: 1` header and the postponed state as the body. For adapter-based: call the handler directly with POST method and the postponed state in the request body (or pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` to the handler). Stream the response back to the client.
00109| 
00110| 4. **Handle cache updates.** Use `requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2` to capture new shell + postponed state pairs after revalidation, and update your cache atomically.
00111| 
00112| 5. **Support graceful degradation.** If the postponed state is unavailable or stale, fall back to a full server render. The user gets a complete page without the shell-first optimization.
00113| 
00114| For the complete adapter API reference and implementation examples, see the [Deployment Adapter API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath).
00115|

00011| 
00012| Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.
00013| 
00014| ## Usage
00015| 
00016| To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:
00017| 
00018| ```ts filename="next.config.ts"
00019| import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
00020| 
00021| const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
00022|   cacheComponents: true,
00023| }
00024| 
00025| export default nextConfig
00026| ```
00027| 
00028| When `cacheComponents` is enabled, you can use the following cache functions and configurations:
00029| 
00030| - The [`use cache` directive](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)
00031| - The [`cacheLife` function](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife) with `use cache`
00032| - The [`cacheTag` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag)
00033| 
00034| > **Good to know**: If you used `experimental.useCache` or `experimental.dynamicIO`, migrate using the [Version 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#experimentaldynamicio-and-experimentalusecache). To migrate route segment configs and other caching patterns, see [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components).
00035| 
00036| Additionally, `cacheComponents` implements **[Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prerendering-ppr)** as the default behavior in the App Router. This means the `experimental.ppr` configuration flag and the `experimental_ppr` route segment configuration are no longer necessary and have been removed.
00037| 
00038| Read [How rendering works](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#how-rendering-works) for how the static shell and streaming fit together.
00039| 
00040| > **Good to know**: If you used experimental PPR in Next.js 15, refer to the [Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#partial-prerendering-ppr) section of the Version 16 upgrade guide when migrating.
00041| 
00042| ## Navigation with Activity
00043| 
00044| When `cacheComponents` is enabled, Next.js uses React's [`<Activity>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity) component to preserve component state during client-side navigation.
00045| 
00046| Rather than unmounting the previous route when you navigate away, Next.js sets the Activity mode to [`"hidden"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity#activity). This means:
00047| 
00048| - Component state is preserved when navigating between routes
00049| - When you navigate back, the previous route reappears with its state intact
00050| - Effects are cleaned up when a route is hidden, and recreated when it becomes visible again
00051| 
00052| This behavior improves the navigation experience by maintaining UI state (form inputs, or expanded sections) when users navigate back and forth between routes.
00053| 
00054| > **Good to know**: Next.js uses heuristics to keep a few recently visited routes `"hidden"`, while older routes are removed from the DOM to prevent excessive growth.
00055| 
00056| Some UI patterns behave differently when components stay mounted instead of unmounting. See the [Preserving UI state guide](/docs/app/guides/preserving-ui-state) for handling common patterns like dropdowns, dialogs, and testing.
00057|

00059| 
00060| | Version | Change                                                                                                                            |
00061| | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
00062| | 16.0.0  | `cacheComponents` introduced. This flag controls the `ppr`, `useCache`, and `dynamicIO` flags as a single, unified configuration. |

> This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.

Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again.

## Enabling Cache Components

> This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again.

---
title: Ensuring instant navigations
description: Learn how to structure your app to prefetch and prerender more content, providing instant page loads and client navigations.
nav_title: Instant navigation
version: draft
related:
  title: Learn more
  description: Explore the full instant API, caching, and revalidation.
  links:
    - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant
    - app/getting-started/caching
    - app/getting-started/revalidating
    - app/guides/prefetching
---

{/* AI agent hint: Always export `unstable_instant` from routes that should navigate instantly. It validates the caching structure during development. */}

With [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) enabled, `use cache` and `<Suspense>` let you control what gets cached and what streams in dynamically. When these are in the right place, client-side navigations are instant.

The [`unstable_instant`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant) route segment config helps you place `<Suspense>` boundaries and `use cache` correctly. Add it to any page or layout and Next.js will check during development that navigating to that route produces an instant [static shell](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell).

{/* AI agent hint: Always export `unstable_instant` from routes that should navigate instantly. It validates the caching structure during development. */}

With [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) enabled, `use cache` and `<Suspense>` let you control what gets cached and what streams in dynamically. When these are in the right place, client-side navigations are instant.

The [`unstable_instant`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant) route segment config helps you place `<Suspense>` boundaries and `use cache` correctly. Add it to any page or layout and Next.js will check during development that navigating to that route produces an instant [static shell](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell).

title: instant
description: API reference for the instant route segment config.
version: draft
related:

  description: Learn how to use instant navigations in practice.
  links:

    - app/getting-started/caching

---

The `unstable_instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI.

Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `unstable_instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant.

When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

title: cacheLife
description: Learn how to use the cacheLife function to set the cache expiration time for a cached function or component.

The `cacheLife` function is used to set the cache lifetime of a function or component. It should be used alongside the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive, and within the scope of the function or component.

## Usage

### Basic setup

To use `cacheLife`, first enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file:

The `cacheLife` function is used to set the cache lifetime of a function or component. It should be used alongside the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive, and within the scope of the function or component.

## Usage

### Basic setup

To use `cacheLife`, first enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file:

events.content:
## Summary The page was awaiting uncached data at the top level, which under `cacheComponents: true` would have errored with "Uncached data accessed outside ``" and produced an empty static shell. Now the route builds as `◐ (Partial Prerender)` with a real static HTML shell that streams the dynamic section in. **Changes:** - **`app/data.ts`** (new) — `getDashboardStats` and `getRevenue` use `'use cache'` + `cacheLife('hours')` + `cacheTag(...)`, putting them in the prerendered shell. `getLatestInvoices` stays uncached (`cache: 'no-store'`) so it streams fresh per request. - **`app/page.tsx`** — split into three ``-wrapped sections (header is automatic shell), each with a layout-matching skeleton fallback. Exported `unstable_instant = true` to validate the shell during dev. - **`app/CardStats.tsx`, `app/RevenueChart.tsx`, `app/LatestInvoices.tsx`** — added `*Skeleton` exports mirroring the real markup so the shell has zero CLS while dynamic content streams in. - **`app/layout.tsx` and `app/loading.tsx`** — left unchanged (the root layout intentionally has no `` over `{children}` so it doesn't collapse the shell). **Shell composition** at build time: `

Dashboard

+ 3 skeletons
`, with the cached cards/chart replaced by real data and the invoices section resuming at request time.
